title: How to run Secret Santa so nobody draws themselves
description:
Put 10 names in a hat and there's a 63% chance at least one person pulls their own; only about 37% of draws come out clean (it's 1 in e, and it stays 63% for 100 or 1,000 people). Redrawing until it works takes almost 3 rounds on average, and about 2 in 5 clean draws still have two people who drew each other. The fix: shuffle the names into a circle and have everyone buy for the next person round. Nobody can get their own name, no two people swap, and it works on the first try. A draw where nobody gets their own is called a derangement; Pierre de Montmort first studied them in 1708.

Numbers checked in code (exact counts and 200,000 simulated hats). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derangement

beats.say: You're running the office Secret Santa, and somebody always draws their own name. Here's how you fix it.
Put 10 names in a hat. The chance that at least one person pulls their own name is 63%.
Each person has a one in 10 shot at their own. 10 small risks stack up. Only 37% of draws come out clean.
So invite more people? With 100 names, it's still 63%. With 1,000, still 63%.
Fine, you redraw until it works. On average, that's almost 3 rounds of everyone digging through a hat.
Uh-oh. Even a clean draw goes wrong. Ben drew Cara, and Cara drew Ben. That happens in about 2 out of 5 clean draws.
Throw out the hat. Shuffle the names into a circle. Everyone buys for the next person round.
Nobody is next to themselves, so nobody gets their own name. No two people swap. It works on the first try.
And there you have it: one shuffle, zero redraws, and the whole office in one big loop.
Mathematicians call a draw where nobody gets their own a derangement. Pierre de Montmort counted them in 1708.
